newsitem.title: FRANCE: Investigators see progress in Paris bomb probe.
newsitem.headline: Investigators see progress in Paris bomb probe.

text.p: Investigators reported progress on Thursday in their hunt for the bomber of a Paris rush-hour commuter train as police and troops patrolled cities and borders to try to prevent more attacks.

Investigators believe they have determined where the perpetrator boarded the train as well as his route, enabling them better to pinpoint where they should search for more clues and witnesses, sources close to the case said.

Police appealed to travellers who used the RER suburban line around the time of Tuesday's blast, in which two people were killed and 91 injured, to contact them on a free telephone number. Twenty-two people were still in hospital on Thursday.

Investigators focused on Algerian militants who are battling the French-backed military government in a war in their homeland that has claimed an estimated 50,000 lives since 1992. In that year, Algieria scrapped elections that Islamic fundamentalists were poised to win.

In a troubling coincidence, according to the Moslem calendar, which relies on lunar cycles, Tuesday's blast fell a day after the second anniversary of the hijacking of an Air France plane in Algiers on Christmas eve 1994 by Moslem gunmen.

After seizing the plane in Algiers, the gunmen killed three passengers and then flew to Marseille, where French commandos stormed the aircraft, killed the hijackers and freed all the passengers being held hostage.
Algerian rebels said their 1995 bomb attacks in France were driven by revenge for the hijackers' killing.
Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre pointed to "extremely worrying similarities" between the attack and last year's bombs.
"There are similarities not only in the make-up of the device but also in the methods used," he told Radio Luxembourg.

Debre cautioned that the bombing investigation would be "necessarily long and difficult" even as he said it would proceed more smoothly due to the experience gained from investigating last year's bombings.
He said France had been at "constant risk" of guerrilla attacks since last year and he dismissed press suggestions that France had ignored warnings of imminent attacks.
"There are today almost 200 Islamists in prison," he said, insisting that investigators had kept up probes and arrests.
French secret agents believe they spotted suspected guerrilla mastermind Ali Touchent, also known as Tarek, in London three weeks ago, sources close to the probe told Reuters.
The authorities believe Tarek was one of the ringleaders of the network which carried out last year's bombings.

Just days before Tuesday's bombing, an anti-terrorism magistrate formally placed two suspected Moslem militants under investigation after bomb components, arms and fundamentalist literature were found in one of their homes in a suburb of Lyon, central France, judicial sources said. The incident was apparently unrelated to the train bombing, the sources said.

In a high-profile show of strength designed to reassure and deter, soldiers and police guarded railway stations in Paris and major cities, and tightened surveillance at borders, airports and tourist sites such as the Eiffel Tower.

A total of 1,870 troops and 1,700 paramilitary gendarmes were ordered out to back up police, 800 of them in Paris. French customs agents were also asked to help by tightening security at borders, ports, airports and railway stations.

Spot checks were made on cars on the Champs-Elysees avenue and guards at stores searched Christmas shoppers' bags. Police handed stickers to travellers on the Metro underground railway urging them to be alert for suspect packages.

The dead in Tuesday's explosion were a newly married Canadian woman, Helene Viel, and a Frenchman from New Caledonia, Lucien Devambez. Viel had arrived in Paris on Sunday with her husband, Frank Stonebanks, to find a flat. Her husband was to be transferred on January 1 from Montreal to the French capital by his employer, U.S. pharmaceutical firm Rhone-Poulenc Rorer.
